segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They dried the black-bound book on Walter Ames's counter, between two bowls of sand, with the shop shutters open to the afternoon. Jory Brennick had never read a thing so slowly in his life. The tide-mark ran across the bottom third of every page and took the figures with it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Fourth trial. Ground stone, one part in forty. Water boiled and stood till cold. Three spoons at the turn of each watch, and nothing to eat for an hour after.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He looked up.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: One part in forty. That's nothing at all. That's a thumbnail in a bucket.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: That's why she burned the first three sets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter had the loupe to his eye and a strip of paper under the line, moving it down a word at a time.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She writes here that the second trial was stronger and did harm. She does not say how much harm. She was not writing for me.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: So you make it up in your back room and try it on somebody.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said it flatly, which was not how he said most things. He set the loupe down.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: I sell bay and camomile and a salve for chilblains. I have never in my life weighed out a part in forty, and I'd be guessing at the grinding. Hartsford has a healer on Dunnock Lane who keeps a balance with brass weights the size of peas. The book goes to her, and the stone with it, wrapped as it is.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: You've waited twenty years to hold that book.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: And my grandmother waited a winter to get the measures right. I'd not spoil her work in an afternoon to say I'd done it myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They walked up to Dunnock Lane before the light went. The healer came to her own door with her sleeves pinned back, and she looked first at the book, then at the sailcloth bundle, then at the four of them standing in her entry like a delegation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter put the book into her hands and began to tell her where it came from.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: It was written by my grandmother. She kept the apothecary's shop on Kettle Row, down in the old town, and her family name was —

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stopped. He tried once more, and the word was not there to try with. His mouth shaped around a gap.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory took half a step forward and Walter held up his hand to stop him. Then he reached into his coat and brought out the oilcloth, and unfolded the letter on the healer's own table, both pages, the bloomed ink and the signature at the foot of it.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: There. That's her hand, and that's the name on it. I find I can't say it aloud any more. You may make of that what you like, but read the second page before you decide.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The healer read the second page standing up, and then sat down and read it again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three days later a girl came down to Floatsome with a note for Jory, which was not a thing that happened often. The healer had made up the draught to the fourth set of measures, one part in forty, and tried it on two households off Cutler Street where the fever had been worst. Both had kept their food down by the second morning. She wanted more of the stone, and she wanted it weighed by her and nobody else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That same morning the hammer frame went out over Kettle Row. Jory stood on the Shoreside walkway and watched Selah Vance's crew drop the first piling into the water above the dyers' yard, on the day she had said it, an hour after the tide turned.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Clear below?

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Clear. Nothing down there now but a post with four empty holes in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames paid him on the platform that evening, counted out full, and then counted a second sum beside it and pushed it across.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: That's for the woman who remembered a lantern that didn't move.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: I'll take it. I'd have told you for nothing, but I'll take it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora Quill sat on the edge of the boards with her heels in the water, looking out past the hulls to where the harbour went dark green and then dark.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: She wants more stone.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: She wants it off the crack itself. Out past the dyers, where the floor opened.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Then that's our next contract, and I'm not being called your partner on it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Co-signed. Both names on the paper.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud said nothing for a while. Then she got up and went for her chart case.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Not until I've been over that ground with a line and drawn it properly. We went down Kettle Row on a chart four years out of date and it nearly cost us the only door that shop had.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: And if the drawing takes a month?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Then the fissure's been there twenty years and it'll keep a month. This time we map it first.
